why: Both patches correctly limit response-based retries to expressions that read response placeholders, including dynamic names. Patch A also adds unrelated `IdleTimeoutWriter` hijack-detachment changes in `idletimeout.go`, which are out of scope, while Patch B stays focused on the retry fix.

Both fix the bug and pass, but B keeps the reverse_proxy-specific placeholder list inside the reverseproxy package and exposes only a generic `PlaceholderNames` accessor, whereas A hardcodes `http.reverse_proxy.*` names into the generic caddyhttp CEL matcher, which is a layering violation a maintainer would not want.

Both patches remove the leaked `File()` dup that kept the old socket listening, and both handle refcounted holders, double close, the close/listen race and abstract sockets; B does it with a simpler single holder-set model, while A keeps a redundant counter alongside the holder map and also changes reuse-path `listenerPool` accounting, which the task didn't ask for.

Patch A meets the hostile-archive requirement: it hides entries nested below a symlink, and name conflicts between a link and a regular `.rclonelink` file, in both zip and squashfs. Patch B still exposes `link/pwn.txt` under a symlink, and its test only passes because the dangling link target happens not to exist.

Both patches fix the leaked dup'd fd, release references only once, and handle the close/listen race with a count-identity check. A does this more simply and limits the abstract-socket exception to Linux, while B adds a `previous`-socket chain that the task does not require and that keeps references to closed sockets for every reload.

Both patches fix the bug correctly: they detect `ph` calls whose static name is a response placeholder and treat dynamic names conservatively, but B does it with less code, while A also adds static string-concatenation folding the task did not require.

Both patches fix the bug the same way: they close the dup'd fd, unlink by the stored path under the mutex, add idempotent `Close` returning `net.ErrClosed`, and guard abstract sockets; A does it with a smaller change that keeps the existing value receivers on the delete wrappers, while B also restructures the state and receivers and adds defensive checks the task does not need.

Patch B explicitly drops zip members that sit beneath a symlink when links are translated, so a hostile archive cannot write outside the destination; Patch A has no such guard and its escape test passes only because of copy ordering in other code. B also keeps the Open clamping limited to symlink objects instead of changing it for every zip member.

Patch A meets every agreed behavior with a smaller change that reuses the existing CEL placeholder helpers, and its tests run all the request-only cases (upstream host, escaped literal, similar name) end to end while keeping coverage of both placeholder syntaxes; Patch B adds speculative string-concatenation folding and swaps the shorthand integration test for the `ph()` form.

Both patches fix the root cause: they close the duplicated fd and unlink the socket under the mutex at the last reference. B keeps the existing reuse return path unchanged, limits the abstract-socket check to Linux/Android so macOS paths starting with '@' are still unlinked before bind, and avoids unlinking a path another tracked socket still uses. A changes reuse to add a pool reference and wrapper, and skips the pre-bind unlink for '@' paths on every OS.

Patch B correctly resolves a root given as the listed `.rclonelink` name in both zip and squashfs, so listing and `NewObject` agree on which names exist, whereas Patch A only treats the unsuffixed name as a single-object root; Patch A's extra escape test is nice but adds no protection code.
